aloevera.traditionalUses: Traditionally applied raw to soothe sunburns, minor thermal burns, acne, and consumed as a gentle digestive and cooling tonic.
aloevera.potentialHealthBenefits: Promotes skin repair, accelerates thermal burn healing, supports gastrointestinal mucosal lining, and hydrates dermal layers.
aloevera.preparationMethods: Fresh transparent inner fillet scooped and applied topically; inner gel blended with water or amla juice for morning tonic.
aloevera.precautions: Avoid yellow outer latex (aloin) during pregnancy and kidney disease. Clear gel itself is gentle and safe.
aloevera.knownToxicity: Inner gel is non-toxic. High-aloin whole leaf extracts should not be chronically ingested.

amla.traditionalUses: Key pillar of Ayurvedic medicine. Central component of Triphala and Chyawanprash, used to rebuild immunity, stimulate digestion, and promote longevity.
amla.potentialHealthBenefits: Exceptionally high bioavailable Vitamin C protects cellular DNA against free radicals, improves lipid balance, and prevents hair thinning.
amla.preparationMethods: Fresh fruit juice taken with a teaspoon of honey; dried fruit powder (churna) taken with warm water; infused herbal hair oils.
amla.precautions: Generally extremely safe. Due to high natural acidity, take after meals if prone to gastric reflux.

amruta_balli.localNames: Guduchi, Amrita, Giloe, Seenthil Kodi, Tippa Teega
amruta_balli.traditionalUses: Known as 'Amrita' (Divine Nectar of Immortality). Extensively prescribed for chronic recurrent fevers, platelet recovery, and metabolic balance.
amruta_balli.potentialHealthBenefits: Enhances macrophage phagocytosis, combats seasonal pyrexia, stimulates platelet production, and improves glycemic control.
amruta_balli.preparationMethods: Decoction (Kashayam) of crushed fresh stems boiled down to 1/4th volume; Guduchi Satva (purified herbal starch).
amruta_balli.precautions: Diabetic patients should monitor blood glucose as it has mild synergistic hypoglycemic action.

arali.traditionalUses: Sacred tree across India. Bark and leaf infusions are traditionally used to heal ulcers, stop internal bleeding, soothe toothaches, and treat respiratory asthma.
arali.potentialHealthBenefits: Tannins promote rapid tissue wound contraction, mitigate oral inflammation, and help regulate glycemic balance.
arali.preparationMethods: Bark decoction used as an astringent oral mouthwash; tender leaves dried and prepared into herbal tea.
arali.precautions: Avoid excessive intake of bark tannins on an empty stomach.
arali.knownToxicity: Leaves and bark are non-toxic at standard culinary/decoction amounts.

ashoka.traditionalUses: Famed Ayurvedic female health tonic. Bark is the foundation of Ashokarishta, traditionally used for heavy menstrual bleeding, fibroids, and uterine cramping.
ashoka.potentialHealthBenefits: Rich in flavonoids and catechins that tonify uterine smooth muscle, relieve pelvic congestion, and reduce dysmenorrhea.
ashoka.preparationMethods: Traditional bark decoction boiled with milk and water (Ashoka Ksheerapaka); Ashokarishta fermented tonic.
ashoka.precautions: Avoid during pregnancy due to uterine stimulating actions. Best taken under female healthcare supervision.

ashwagandha.localNames: Asgandh, Winter Cherry, Kanaje Hindi, Penneru
ashwagandha.traditionalUses: Premier vitality Rasayana herb in Ayurveda, used for centuries to combat chronic stress, improve sleep architecture, and increase physical endurance.
ashwagandha.potentialHealthBenefits: Lowers serum cortisol, enhances cognitive retention and focus, modulates GABAergic signaling, and supports thyroid hormone balance.
ashwagandha.preparationMethods: Finely milled root powder (Churna) boiled in warm milk with nutmeg; standardized root extract capsules.
ashwagandha.precautions: Avoid during pregnancy. Consult physician if on thyroid medications or central nervous system depressants.
ashwagandha.knownToxicity: Non-toxic at standard supplemental dosages (300-600mg extract/day).

avacado.traditionalUses: Leaves are brewed as herbal teas in traditional folk medicine for hypertension, urinary complaints, and soothing joint aches.
avacado.potentialHealthBenefits: High in monounsaturated oleic acid, quercetin, and lutein supporting cardiovascular endothelial integrity and ocular health.
avacado.preparationMethods: Leaf infusion (tea) for mild diuretic and soothing support; nutrient-rich fruit pulp consumed fresh.
avacado.precautions: Avocado leaves contain persin, which can be toxic to domestic pets (birds, horses, dogs). Safe for human culinary consumption.
avacado.knownToxicity: Fruit pulp and mild leaf teas are non-toxic for humans.

bamboo.traditionalUses: Siliceous secretion (Tabashir / Vanshlochan) harvested from bamboo internodes is prized in Ayurveda for bone strength, respiratory vitality, and cough relief.
bamboo.potentialHealthBenefits: Over 70% bioavailable plant organic silica stimulates bone mineralization, collagen generation, and strengthens nails and hair.
bamboo.preparationMethods: Purified Vanshlochan powder blended with honey for respiratory health; young edible shoots boiled in curries.
bamboo.precautions: Raw bamboo shoots must always be boiled to remove cyanogenic glycosides before eating.
bamboo.knownToxicity: Cooked shoots and purified Vanshlochan are non-toxic.

basale.localNames: Basale, Pui Saag, Bacchali, Kodip Pasali
basale.traditionalUses: Succulent climbing green widely eaten across India to cool the body, relieve mouth ulcers, prevent constipation, and heal gastritis.
basale.potentialHealthBenefits: Dense mucilage coats gastric mucosa, reducing heartburn while providing rich bioavailable iron and provitamin A.
basale.preparationMethods: Cooked into cooling curries, dal (Basale Sambhar), or blended into fresh leaf juices.

betel.traditionalUses: Chewed post-meals across India to stimulate salivary and gastric secretions, eliminate halitosis, and soothe chest congestion in infants.
betel.potentialHealthBenefits: High in eugenol and hydroxychavicol, which neutralize anaerobic oral pathogens, relieve flatulence, and improve digestion.
betel.preparationMethods: Chewed fresh plain (without tobacco/areca nut); leaf warmed with castor oil applied on chest for infant phlegm.
betel.precautions: Plain leaf is very beneficial. Do NOT combine with tobacco or chemical additives.
betel.knownToxicity: Pure green leaf is non-toxic and culinary.

betel_nut.traditionalUses: Historically used in traditional systems in micro-quantities for expelling tapeworms and increasing digestive secretions.
betel_nut.potentialHealthBenefits: Contains alkaloids such as arecoline that stimulate muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
betel_nut.precautions: WHO classifies chronic habitual chewing of areca nut as a known oral carcinogen. Internal regular consumption is strongly discouraged.
betel_nut.knownToxicity: Contains cytotoxic and genotoxic alkaloids. Not recommended for routine medicinal self-care.

brahmi.traditionalUses: Celebrated Medhya Rasayana herb taken by Ayurvedic scholars to sharpen memory, improve recall speed, enhance speech, and calm anxiety.
brahmi.potentialHealthBenefits: Bacosides cross the blood-brain barrier to repair damaged neurons, enhance synaptic neurotransmission, and mitigate mental fatigue.
brahmi.preparationMethods: Fresh juice (swarasa) with ghee; Brahmi Ghrita (clarified butter infusion); standardized bacoside extract.
brahmi.precautions: Safe. Mild stomach upset or nausea may occur if taken on an empty stomach; best consumed with healthy fats (ghee/milk).

castor.traditionalUses: Castor oil is one of the most powerful Ayurvedic laxatives for detoxifying the colon (Virechana). Warmed leaves are wrapped around swollen arthritic joints to relieve acute pain.
castor.potentialHealthBenefits: Ricinoleic acid binds to EP3 prostanoid receptors on smooth muscle, stimulating peristalsis and relieving joint swelling.
castor.preparationMethods: Leaves warmed with oil applied externally to joint swellings; cold-pressed, detoxified castor oil for medicinal purge.
castor.precautions: Raw castor seeds contain ricin, a lethal poison. NEVER eat unprocessed raw castor seeds. Castor oil must be avoided in pregnancy.
castor.knownToxicity: Raw seeds are extremely poisonous. Purified pharmaceutical oil is ricin-free and safe under dosage guidelines.

curry_leaf.localNames: Kadi Patta, Kariveppila, Meetha Neem, Karuvappilai
curry_leaf.traditionalUses: Essential staple of Indian cuisine and Siddha/Ayurvedic medicine for stimulating digestive agni, treating dysentery, and preventing premature hair graying.
curry_leaf.potentialHealthBenefits: Supports pancreatic beta-cell function, prevents oxidative breakdown of lipids, and fortifies hair roots with iron, beta-carotene, and protein.
curry_leaf.preparationMethods: Chewing 8-10 raw fresh leaves early morning; paste applied as scalp mask with yogurt; leaves infused into coconut oil for hair tonic.

doddapatre.localNames: Doddapatre, Karpuravalli, Patharchur, Mexican Mint, Cuban Oregano, Vamu Aku
doddapatre.traditionalUses: Household remedy across South India for relieving acute colds, wet coughs, infantile asthma, and indigestion. Succulent leaves are warmed and pressed.
doddapatre.potentialHealthBenefits: Relaxes respiratory smooth muscle spasms, liquifies tenacious bronchial mucus, and relieves gas and bloating.
doddapatre.preparationMethods: Leaf gently warmed on dry tawa and pressed to extract fresh juice with a drop of honey; fried in chickpea batter (Doddapatre Bajji) for easy pediatric dosing.
doddapatre.precautions: Gentle and very safe for both children and adults.

ekka.traditionalUses: Leaves warmed with sesame oil applied externally over joints to relieve severe rheumatic pain and reduce inflammatory swelling.
ekka.potentialHealthBenefits: Cardiac glycosides and latex enzymes cause localized circulatory stimulation and analgesia when applied on intact skin.
ekka.preparationMethods: External poultice of oiled, warmed leaves. NEVER ingest fresh milky latex.
ekka.precautions: Milky latex is irritating to eyes and toxic internally. Wash hands thoroughly after handling. Not for internal consumption.
ekka.knownToxicity: Latex contains calotropin and uscharin which are cardiac poisons if ingested.

ganike.traditionalUses: Famous in South India for curing recurrent oral and stomach ulcers. Soup of tender leaves is cooked to restore liver health following jaundice.
ganike.potentialHealthBenefits: Inhibits gastric acid secretion, strengthens mucosal defense barriers, and shields hepatocytes against chemical injury.
ganike.preparationMethods: Cooked leaf soup (Manathakkali Saaru) taken with steamed rice; sun-dried ripe berries (Vathal).
ganike.precautions: Only eat mature, cooked leaves and fully ripe black berries. Do NOT eat raw unripe green berries.
ganike.knownToxicity: Unripe green berries contain toxic solanine.

gauva.traditionalUses: Tender leaves are chewed across India to cure toothaches, bleeding gums, and prepared into a tea to stop acute watery diarrhea.
gauva.potentialHealthBenefits: Tannins bind to rotavirus and bacterial toxins, halting gastrointestinal hypermotility, while flavonoids inhibit alpha-glucosidase to modulate sugar spikes.
gauva.preparationMethods: Tender leaf tea (boiled 5 minutes in water); chewing 2-3 young leaves for gum strengthening.

geranium.traditionalUses: Aromatic leaves used in balms and herbal steam for clearing sinus headaches and harmonizing nervous anxiety.
geranium.potentialHealthBenefits: Geraniol and citronellol inhibit microbial growth and promote peaceful neurological states.
geranium.preparationMethods: Herbal steam inhalation; leaf infused in hot water for relaxing bath.
geranium.precautions: Safe. Essential oil should be diluted in carrier oil.

henna.traditionalUses: Applied to palms and feet during hot summers to cool the body. Applied as a scalp pack to heal dandruff, fungal tinea, and condition hair cuticle.
henna.potentialHealthBenefits: Lawsone molecule binds with hair keratin, creating a natural protective shield while suppressing Malassezia scalp yeast.
henna.preparationMethods: Fresh leaves crushed with lemon juice into paste; applied to hair or skin for 1-2 hours.
henna.precautions: Natural pure green henna is extremely safe. Avoid chemical 'black henna' containing toxic PPD dye.

hibiscus.localNames: Sembaruthi, Gudhal, Dasavala, Japa Pushpa, Mandara
hibiscus.traditionalUses: Classic Ayurvedic hair remedy. Leaves and red flowers are crushed into a slippery lather to cleanse scalp, stop hair fall, and cool the body.
hibiscus.potentialHealthBenefits: Rich in mucilage, flavonoids, and fruit acids that hydrate scalp skin, prevent dandruff, and promote hair shaft diameter.
hibiscus.preparationMethods: Fresh leaves crushed with water into natural conditioning shampoo; flower tea for cardiovascular wellness.

honge.traditionalUses: Widely used in Ayurveda for stubborn dermatological conditions (scabies, eczema, ringworm, leprosy wounds). Oil is applied topically.
honge.potentialHealthBenefits: Pongapin and furanoflavonoids eradicate cutaneous mites, fungi, and accelerate epithelial regeneration.
honge.preparationMethods: External application of Karanja seed oil diluted with coconut oil; leaf paste applied to fungal skin patches.
honge.precautions: For external use only. Seed oil should not be ingested.
honge.knownToxicity: Karanja oil is toxic if swallowed internally in quantity.

insulin.localNames: Insulin Plant, Step Ladder, Spiral Flag
insulin.traditionalUses: Famous in contemporary Indian ethnomedicine. Diabetics chew 1-2 fresh succulent leaves daily to help manage elevated fasting blood sugar.
insulin.potentialHealthBenefits: Corosolic acid and bioactive triterpenoids promote peripheral glucose uptake and enhance insulin sensitivity.
insulin.preparationMethods: Chewing 1 fresh leaf in the morning and 1 in the evening; dried leaf powder in hot water.
insulin.precautions: Regularly monitor blood glucose levels to prevent hypoglycemic episodes when combined with prescribed diabetic medication.
insulin.knownToxicity: Safe at recommended culinary dosage (1-2 leaves/day).

jasmine.traditionalUses: Flowers and leaves applied on hot skin rashes, eye fatigue, and brewed as tea to calm emotional agitation.
jasmine.potentialHealthBenefits: Linalool and benzyl acetate exert calming effects on autonomic nervous system arousal via olfactory pathway.
jasmine.preparationMethods: Aqueous flower infusion for eye wash; herbal tea; infused topical oil.

lemon.traditionalUses: Crushed lemon leaves inhaled to relieve nausea, travel sickness, and morning fatigue. Juice consumed to aid hepatic detox.
lemon.potentialHealthBenefits: Citric acid prevents renal calcium oxalate stones while flavonoids optimize vascular capillary permeability.
lemon.preparationMethods: Fresh juice in lukewarm water; crushed leaf tea for stomach ease.

lemon_grass.traditionalUses: Classic herbal tea across tropics for breaking fevers through sweating, easing indigestion, and calming headaches.
lemon_grass.potentialHealthBenefits: Citral and myrcene inhibit cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) pathways to reduce musculoskeletal pain and microbial infection.
lemon_grass.preparationMethods: Boiled in water with ginger for herbal tea; aromatic steam for respiratory congestion.
lemon_grass.precautions: Safe. Avoid excessive essential oil during pregnancy.

mango.traditionalUses: Tender purple/green leaves are boiled into tea in folk Ayurveda to manage early-stage diabetes and lower blood pressure.
mango.potentialHealthBenefits: Mangiferin inhibits carbohydrate digestive enzymes, protects pancreatic beta cells, and improves arterial compliance.
mango.preparationMethods: Boil 5-6 fresh tender leaves in water, leave overnight, and drink strained water in the morning.

mint.traditionalUses: Widely used in chutneys, teas, and summer tonics to prevent heat stroke, reduce nausea, and relieve abdominal cramping.
mint.potentialHealthBenefits: Menthol relaxes visceral smooth muscles, alleviating indigestion and bloating while clearing nasal passages.
mint.preparationMethods: Fresh leaf infusion in hot or cold water; blended into refreshing digestive mint chutney.

nagadali.traditionalUses: Folk remedy for colic, infantile spasms, and rheumatic aches. Pungent aromatic leaves placed around infants to repel insects.
nagadali.potentialHealthBenefits: Rutin and coumarins exert anti-inflammatory and microvascular strengthening effects.
nagadali.preparationMethods: External compress; oil infusion for earache. Internal usage should be strictly limited.
nagadali.precautions: Strongly contraindicated in pregnancy as it can induce uterine contractions and abortion. Can cause phototoxic dermatitis.
nagadali.knownToxicity: Toxic internally in large amounts. Handle with gloves in bright sunlight.

neem.localNames: Nimba, Arishta, Veppamaram, Indian Lilac, Vepa
neem.traditionalUses: Known as 'the village pharmacy'. Leaves, bark, and seeds are traditionally used for purifying blood, managing eczema, psoriasis, acne, and oral health.
neem.potentialHealthBenefits: Inhibits dermatological pathogens, prevents plaque and gum infections, and supports liver detoxification.
neem.preparationMethods: Fresh leaf paste applied on dermal blemishes; leaf bath for itching skin; bark water decoction for oral gargle.
neem.precautions: Internal use of seed oil is contraindicated in infants, children, and pregnant women. Leaves in moderation are safe.
neem.knownToxicity: Neem seed oil is toxic if ingested internally in large quantities.

nithyapushpa.traditionalUses: In folk medicine, 2-3 fresh leaves are chewed in the morning to lower blood sugar. Modern medicine extracts vincristine and vinblastine for chemotherapy.
nithyapushpa.potentialHealthBenefits: Contains over 130 indole alkaloids that influence carbohydrate metabolism and inhibit cancer cell mitosis.
nithyapushpa.preparationMethods: Herbal infusion of 2 leaves in water for diabetes.
nithyapushpa.precautions: Should only be taken in small micro-doses under supervision. Avoid in pregnancy and liver disease.
nithyapushpa.knownToxicity: Contains cytotoxic vinca alkaloids; toxic in overdose.

nooni.traditionalUses: Traditional Polynesian and Ayurvedic fruit used for chronic fatigue, joint stiffness, immune deficiency, and general vitality.
nooni.potentialHealthBenefits: Rich in proxeronine, scopoletin, and polysaccharides that modulate immune cytokines and provide natural pain relief.
nooni.preparationMethods: Fermented fresh fruit juice taken in morning on empty stomach with warm water.
nooni.precautions: High potassium content; patients with chronic kidney disease should consult a doctor before consuming.
nooni.knownToxicity: Fruit juice is safe for general consumption.

pappaya.traditionalUses: Famed emergency remedy for dengue fever. Fresh leaf juice is extracted and given to rapidly increase low blood platelet counts.
pappaya.potentialHealthBenefits: Carpaine and flavonoids upregulate ALOX12 and PTAFR genes, stimulating megakaryocytes in bone marrow to release blood platelets.
pappaya.preparationMethods: Wash fresh mature leaves thoroughly, crush with mortar-pestle (without water), and squeeze 20-30ml pure juice twice daily.
pappaya.precautions: Juice has a very bitter taste. Avoid unripe papaya and excessive leaf juice during pregnancy as it contains latex that can stimulate uterine contractions.
pappaya.knownToxicity: Leaves are non-toxic at therapeutic dosages.

pepper.traditionalUses: The 'King of Spices'. Used to kindle digestive agni, clear respiratory phlegm, and dramatically boost absorption of other medicinal herbs (e.g. Curcumin).
pepper.potentialHealthBenefits: Piperine inhibits intestinal glucuronidation enzymes, dramatically enhancing the systemic bioavailability of vitamins, minerals, and phytonutrients.
pepper.preparationMethods: Freshly ground pepper boiled with milk and turmeric for cold relief; culinary seasoning.

pomegranate.traditionalUses: Peel and leaf decoction is an ancient Ayurvedic remedy for dysentery, diarrhea, and strengthening bleeding gums.
pomegranate.potentialHealthBenefits: Ellagitannins are metabolized by gut bacteria into urolithin A, which promotes cellular mitophagy and slows aging.
pomegranate.preparationMethods: Fruit juice for heart health; dried rind boiled in water for intestinal upset.

raktachandini.localNames: Rakta Chandana, Lal Chandan, Erra Chandanam, Shenchandanam
raktachandini.traditionalUses: Endangered medicinal tree of South India. Wood paste is applied on skin to clear acne, stubborn dark spots, sunburns, and cool fevers.
raktachandini.potentialHealthBenefits: Santalin flavonoids inhibit tyrosinase to even skin pigmentation and suppress dermal prostaglandins.
raktachandini.preparationMethods: Heartwood rubbed on wet stone with rose water to make fine paste; applied as face mask.
raktachandini.precautions: Safe for external cosmetic and medicinal application.

rose.traditionalUses: Rose petal jam (Gulkand) is eaten throughout summer to prevent nosebleeds, reduce acidity, and relieve constipation.
rose.potentialHealthBenefits: Natural flavonoids soothe gastric lining, calm emotional stress, and protect ocular surface tissues.
rose.preparationMethods: Gulkand (sun-cooked rose petals with sugar); pure steam-distilled rose water for eyes and skin.

sapota.traditionalUses: Tender leaves brewed into herbal tea for fevers and diarrhea. High-energy fruit given to recovering patients.
sapota.potentialHealthBenefits: Rich in natural fructose, dietary fiber, and tannins with natural anti-inflammatory and antiviral actions.
sapota.preparationMethods: Fresh fruit eaten ripe; leaf infusion for digestive support.
sapota.precautions: Safe. Seeds are hard and should be discarded.

tulasi.localNames: Tulasi, Surasa, Krishna Tulsi, Rama Tulsi, Holy Basil
tulasi.traditionalUses: Revered across India as the sacred 'Queen of Herbs'. Extensively used for bronchial relief, coughs, colds, viral fever recovery, and stress resilience.
tulasi.potentialHealthBenefits: Relieves cold and congestion, modulates cellular antioxidant levels, and balances autonomic stress responses.
tulasi.preparationMethods: Fresh leaf decoction/tea with ginger and honey; chewing 4-5 fresh leaves daily on an empty stomach.
tulasi.precautions: May slightly reduce blood glucose; monitor if taking anti-diabetic medication.
tulasi.knownToxicity: Non-toxic herbal food and tea botanical.

wood_sorel.localNames: Changeri, Teen Patti, Puli Chintaku, Puliyarai
wood_sorel.traditionalUses: Classic Ayurvedic remedy for bleeding hemorrhoids, chronic diarrhea, and lack of appetite. Sour leaves cooked with lentils.
wood_sorel.potentialHealthBenefits: Stimulates bile and gastric juices, tightens mucosal capillaries, and remedies mild vitamin deficiencies.
wood_sorel.preparationMethods: Fresh leaves cooked with dal or buttermilk; fresh leaf juice with rock candy for piles.
wood_sorel.precautions: Contains oxalic acid. Individuals with calcium oxalate kidney stones should consume in moderation.
